key_terms.meaning: Full equilibrium with the surroundings: T₀, p₀, at rest, at the reference height, chemically like the surroundings; exergy is zero there.
AE = Q(1 − T₀/T) for a source at constant T; AE = Q − T₀ΔS in general, in kJ.
UE = T₀ΔS: the heat that must go to the surroundings even from a reversible engine.
T₀Q(1/T₂ − 1/T₁) = T₀S<sub>gen</sub> when heat Q falls from T₁ to T₂.
φ = (u − u₀) + p₀(v − v₀) − T₀(s − s₀), in kJ/kg.
ψ = (h − h₀) − T₀(s − s₀) + V²/2 + gz, in kJ/kg.
I = T₀S<sub>gen</sub> (Gouy-Stodola theorem), never negative.
η<sub>II</sub> = exergy recovered ÷ exergy supplied; 1 for a reversible device.
M dx + N dy is exact when (∂M/∂y)<sub>x</sub> = (∂N/∂x)<sub>y</sub>; then it is the differential of a property.
(∂x/∂y)<sub>z</sub> = 1/(∂y/∂x)<sub>z</sub>.
(∂x/∂y)<sub>z</sub>(∂y/∂z)<sub>x</sub>(∂z/∂x)<sub>y</sub> = −1.
A = U − TS; dA = −S dT − p dV; −ΔA is the largest work at constant T.
G = H − TS; dG = −S dT + V dp; −ΔG is the largest non-pV work at constant T and p.
(∂T/∂V)<sub>S</sub> = −(∂p/∂S)<sub>V</sub>, (∂T/∂p)<sub>S</sub> = (∂V/∂S)<sub>p</sub>, (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = (∂p/∂T)<sub>V</sub>, (∂S/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = −(∂V/∂T)<sub>p</sub>.
T ds = c<sub>v</sub>dT + T(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub>dv; T ds = c<sub>p</sub>dT − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>dp.
dp/dT = h₁₂/(T·v₁₂) for any phase boundary.
ln(p₂/p₁) = −(h<sub>fg</sub>/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁), with an ideal vapour and constant h<sub>fg</sub>.
β = (1/v)(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>, in 1/K; 1/T for an ideal gas.
κ<sub>T</sub> = −(1/v)(∂v/∂p)<sub>T</sub>, in 1/Pa; 1/p for an ideal gas.
c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = Tvβ²/κ<sub>T</sub>; equal to R for an ideal gas.
μ<sub>JT</sub> = (∂T/∂p)<sub>h</sub> = [T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> − v]/c<sub>p</sub>; zero for an ideal gas.

takeaways: Of heat Q from a source at T, only Q(1 − T₀/T) can become work; the rest, T₀ΔS, must go to the surroundings.
Heat that falls in temperature loses available energy equal to T₀S<sub>gen</sub>, even though no energy is lost.
Exergy is measured from the dead state and is destroyed at the rate T₀S<sub>gen</sub>; second law efficiency compares a device with the reversible one, not with the energy input.
A property has an exact differential; heat and work do not. The cyclic relation carries a minus sign: the product of the three slopes is −1.
At constant T and V a process can go on its own only if A falls; at constant T and p only if G falls.
Maxwell relations turn entropy slopes into p–v–T slopes, and the TdS equations turn them into entropy, energy and enthalpy changes of real substances.
Along a phase boundary the Gibbs functions of the two phases are equal, which gives the Clapeyron slope h₁₂/(T·v₁₂).
c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = Tvβ²/κ<sub>T</sub> is never negative and equals R for an ideal gas.
A gas cools in a throttle only below its inversion temperature, where μ<sub>JT</sub> > 0; an ideal gas does not change temperature at all.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask the Maxwell relations, the TdS equations, the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, the Mayer relation and the Joule-Thomson coefficient as derivations, and available energy and exergy as numerical problems with the steam tables. Some syllabi teach exergy with the second law and the relations as a separate unit; the questions below cover both.

bank.q: Derive the available and unavailable energy of heat Q taken (a) from a source at constant temperature T and (b) from a finite body that cools from T₁ to T₂, with surroundings at T₀. Show that heat transfer across a finite temperature difference always lowers the available energy.
outline: A reversible engine between the source and T₀ gives the most work
AE = Q(1 − T₀/T), UE = T₀ΔS
Finite body: integrate δQ(1 − T₀/T) to get AE = Q − T₀ΔS
T–s diagram: area above T₀ is AE
Loss in a transfer from T₁ to T₂ is T₀Q(1/T₂ − 1/T₁) = T₀S<sub>gen</sub> > 0
A numerical check
answer: The idea. The only sink is the surroundings at T₀. The most work any heat can give comes from a reversible engine that takes the heat at the temperature it is supplied and rejects heat at T₀. That work is the available energy (AE); the heat the engine must reject is the unavailable energy (UE).

(a) Source at constant T. A Carnot engine between T and T₀ has efficiency 1 − T₀/T. So AE = Q(1 − T₀/T). The rest is UE = Q − AE = Q·T₀/T. The source gives up entropy ΔS = Q/T, so UE = T₀ΔS and AE = Q − T₀ΔS.
On a T–s diagram the source line is horizontal at T, and Q is the rectangle T × ΔS under it. The line T = T₀ splits the rectangle: the part above is AE and the part below, T₀ × ΔS, is UE.

answer.text: (b) Finite body. A body of mass m and specific heat c cools from T₁ to T₂. A small amount δQ = −m·c·dT given at the present temperature T can give at most δW = δQ(1 − T₀/T). Add up all the parts:
answer.pre:
AE = ∫ δQ − T₀ ∫ δQ/T
   = m·c·(T₁ − T₂) − T₀·m·c·ln(T₁/T₂)
   = Q − T₀ΔS,   with ΔS = m·c·ln(T₁/T₂)

answer: Meaning. The same form AE = Q − T₀ΔS holds for any source, where ΔS is the entropy the source gives up. On the T–s diagram the supply curve slopes down, and AE is the area between the curve and the T₀ line.

Transfer across a temperature difference. Let heat Q leave a reservoir at T₁ and enter a body at T₂ < T₁. Before the transfer AE₁ = Q(1 − T₀/T₁); after it AE₂ = Q(1 − T₀/T₂). The loss is AE₁ − AE₂ = T₀Q(1/T₂ − 1/T₁). Since T₂ < T₁, 1/T₂ > 1/T₁ and the loss is positive. The entropy generated is Sgen = Q/T₂ − Q/T₁, so the loss equals T₀Sgen.

head: Case
Data
Result
rows: 1000 kJ from 1000 K to 500 K, T₀ = 300 K

answer: Conclusion. Energy is conserved in a heat transfer, but its available part falls whenever the heat drops in temperature. Heat should therefore be used at the highest temperature it is available and moved across the smallest practical temperature difference.

bank.q: Define exergy and the dead state. Derive the exergy of a closed system and the flow exergy of a steady stream, and show that the exergy destroyed in any process equals T₀S<sub>gen</sub>.
outline: Exergy: largest useful work while coming to the dead state, heat exchanged only with the surroundings
Dead state: T₀, p₀, at rest, reference height, chemical equilibrium
Closed system: first law plus entropy balance, subtract p₀ work: φ = (u − u₀) + p₀(v − v₀) − T₀(s − s₀)
Steady stream: ψ = (h − h₀) − T₀(s − s₀) + V²/2 + gz
Real process: W<sub>u</sub> = W<sub>rev</sub> − T₀S<sub>gen</sub>
Numbers: tank 60.50 kJ/kg, turbine 60 kJ/kg destroyed
answer: Definitions. The dead state is full equilibrium with the surroundings: temperature T₀, pressure p₀, at rest, at the reference height and chemically like the surroundings. Exergy is the largest useful work a system or stream can give as it comes to the dead state, exchanging heat only with the surroundings.

answer.text: Closed system: the two balances. Let the system go from its state to the dead state, exchanging heat δQ with the surroundings at T₀ and doing work δW. The entropy of system plus surroundings can only rise by the generated entropy δSgen:
answer.pre:
First law:  δQ − δW = dU
Entropy:    dS − δQ/T₀ = δS<sub>gen</sub>   so   δQ = T₀dS − T₀δS<sub>gen</sub>
Work:       δW = −dU + T₀dS − T₀δS<sub>gen</sub>

answer.text: Integrate from the state (U, V, S) to the dead state (U₀, V₀, S₀) and remove the work done on the atmosphere, p₀(V₀ − V), which is not useful:
answer.pre:
W = (U − U₀) − T₀(S − S₀) − T₀S<sub>gen</sub>
W<sub>u</sub> = W − p₀(V₀ − V) = (U − U₀) + p₀(V − V₀) − T₀(S − S₀) − T₀S<sub>gen</sub>

answer: Largest useful work. Sgen ≥ 0, so Wu is largest when Sgen = 0. That largest value is the exergy: Φ = (U − U₀) + p₀(V − V₀) − T₀(S − S₀), or per kg φ = (u − u₀) + p₀(v − v₀) − T₀(s − s₀).

answer.text: Steady stream. Per kg of flow, with heat q exchanged only with the surroundings and kinetic and potential energy included:
answer.pre:
Energy:   q − w = (h₂ − h₁) + (V₂² − V₁²)/2 + g(z₂ − z₁)
Entropy:  s₂ − s₁ = q/T₀ + s<sub>gen</sub>   so   q = T₀(s₂ − s₁) − T₀s<sub>gen</sub>
Work:     w = [(h₁ − T₀s₁) − (h₂ − T₀s₂)] + (V₁² − V₂²)/2 + g(z₁ − z₂) − T₀s<sub>gen</sub>

answer: Flow exergy. Let the exit be the dead state (h₀, s₀, at rest, z = 0) and set sgen = 0. The largest work is ψ = (h − h₀) − T₀(s − s₀) + V²/2 + gz. There is no separate p₀ term, because the flow work pv is already inside h.

Exergy destroyed. Between two states the reversible useful work is Wrev = Φ₁ − Φ₂ (or ψ₁ − ψ₂ per kg for a stream). The integration above shows that a real process delivers Wu = Wrev − T₀Sgen. So the exergy destroyed is I = Wrev − Wu = T₀Sgen, the Gouy-Stodola theorem. It is never negative.

Working
Result

bank.q: What is an exact differential? State and prove the test for exactness. Derive the reciprocity and cyclic relations among p, v and T, and verify the cyclic relation for air as an ideal gas at 300 K and 100 kPa.
outline: Total differential dz = M dx + N dy
Exact when it is the differential of a function; test (∂M/∂y)<sub>x</sub> = (∂N/∂x)<sub>y</sub> from equal mixed derivatives
Properties are exact; δq and δw are not; 1/T as integrating factor
Derive reciprocity and the cyclic relation from x(y, z) and y(x, z)
Numerical check with v = 0.861 m³/kg
answer: Total differential. For a simple compressible substance any property z depends on two independent properties x and y. A small change gives dz = (∂z/∂x)ydx + (∂z/∂y)xdy = M dx + N dy.

Exact differential. An expression M dx + N dy is exact when it is the differential of some function z(x, y). Its integral between two states then does not depend on the path, and its integral round a cycle is zero.

The test. If z exists, M = ∂z/∂x and N = ∂z/∂y. Then (∂M/∂y)x = ∂²z/∂y∂x and (∂N/∂x)y = ∂²z/∂x∂y. For a smooth function the mixed derivatives are equal, so an exact differential must satisfy (∂M/∂y)x = (∂N/∂x)y; when the test holds, such a z can be built by integration.

Heat is not exact, entropy is. For an ideal gas, δq = cvdT + (RT/v)dv: ∂(cv)/∂v = 0 but ∂(RT/v)/∂T = R/v, so δq fails the test. ds = δq/T = (cv/T)dT + (R/v)dv passes, since both cross-derivatives are zero. Between 300 K, 0.861 m³/kg and 600 K, 1.722 m³/kg, q is 334.8 kJ/kg on one path and 275.1 kJ/kg on another, while Δs = 0.6966 kJ/(kg·K) on both.

answer.text: Reciprocity and cyclic relations. Let x, y, z be linked by one equation, so x = x(y, z) and y = y(x, z):

answer: Match coefficients. x and z are independent, so the coefficient of dx is 1 and that of dz is 0. The first gives the reciprocity relation (∂x/∂y)z = 1/(∂y/∂x)z. The second gives (∂x/∂y)z(∂y/∂z)x = −(∂x/∂z)y = −1/(∂z/∂x)y, which is the cyclic relation (∂x/∂y)z(∂y/∂z)x(∂z/∂x)y = −1. For p, v, T: (∂p/∂v)T(∂v/∂T)p(∂T/∂p)v = −1.

answer.text: Check for air (R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K), T = 300 K, p = 100 kPa, so v = RT/p = 0.861 m³/kg):

answer: Closing check. Reciprocity: (∂p/∂T)v = R/v = 0.3333 kPa/K, and 0.3333 × 3.000 = 1.000. Both relations hold to four figures. The cyclic product is −1, not +1, because each slope is taken along a different line on the property surface.

bank.q: Define the Helmholtz and Gibbs functions and derive their differentials. Show that −ΔA is the largest work at constant temperature and −ΔG the largest useful (non-pV) work at constant temperature and pressure, and state the conditions for spontaneous change and equilibrium.
outline: A = U − TS, G = H − TS, both properties
dA = −S dT − p dV, dG = −S dT + V dp
First law with Q ≤ TΔS at constant T gives W ≤ −ΔA
At constant p, W<sub>u</sub> ≤ −ΔG
Criteria: ΔA ≤ 0 at constant T, V; ΔG ≤ 0 at constant T, p; minimum at equilibrium
Numerical illustration
answer: Definitions. Helmholtz function A = U − TS; Gibbs function G = H − TS, with H = U + pV. Both are made of properties, so both are properties, in kJ (a and g per kg in kJ/kg).

answer.text: Differentials, from dU = T dS − p dV and dH = T dS + V dp:
answer.pre:
dA = dU − T dS − S dT = −S dT − p dV
dG = dH − T dS − S dT = −S dT + V dp

answer: Natural variables. A is naturally a function of T and V, G of T and p, which are the variables a laboratory or a plant can hold fixed.

answer.text: Largest work at constant T. A closed system exchanges heat Q with surroundings at its own temperature T and does work W:
answer.pre:
First law:  W = Q − ΔU
Entropy:    ΔS − Q/T ≥ 0   so   Q ≤ TΔS
Hence:      W ≤ TΔS − ΔU = −(ΔU − TΔS) = −ΔA

answer: Largest useful work at constant T and p. Split W into the work against the pressure, pΔV, and the useful work Wu. Then Wu ≤ −ΔA − pΔV = −(ΔU + pΔV − TΔS) = −ΔG. A fuel cell or battery delivers at most −ΔG as electrical work.

Criteria. If no work is taken (W = 0 at constant T and V, or Wu = 0 at constant T and p), a process can happen only if ΔA ≤ 0 or ΔG ≤ 0 respectively. The equality holds at equilibrium, which is the minimum of A or of G. A process with ΔG > 0 at constant T and p cannot go on its own; its reverse can.

head: Process
Working
Result
rows: 1 kg air compressed at 300 K, 100 → 500 kPa
ΔA = ΔG = +138.6 kJ: at least 138.6 kJ of work needed
Δg = −12.2 kJ/kg: freezes on its own

answer: Closing check. For the air, the reversible isothermal work mRT·ln(p₂/p₁) = 0.287 × 300 × 1.6094 = 138.6 kJ equals −ΔA in size, as the bound requires for a reversible process.

bank.q: Derive the four Maxwell relations from the exact differentials of U, H, A and G. Explain how two of them give entropy changes from p–v–T data, and use one to find the entropy change of air compressed isothermally at 300 K from 1 bar to 5 bar.
outline: dU, dH, dA, dG as exact differentials
Exactness test on each gives one relation
Table of the four with signs
The A and G relations put entropy slopes in terms of (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> and (∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>
Ideal gas: Δs = −R ln(p₂/p₁) = −0.4619 kJ/(kg·K)
answer: Starting point. For a simple compressible system the four potentials have the exact differentials dU = T dS − p dV, dH = T dS + V dp, dA = −S dT − p dV and dG = −S dT + V dp. Each has the form M dx + N dy, and exactness requires (∂M/∂y)x = (∂N/∂x)y.

Signs. For A, the test gives ∂(−S)/∂V = ∂(−p)/∂T, and the two minus signs cancel. For G, ∂(−S)/∂p = ∂V/∂T, so one minus sign remains. Re-deriving from the potential is safer than memorising the signs.

Why they matter. Entropy cannot be measured directly, but p, v and T can. The A relation (∂s/∂v)T = (∂p/∂T)v gives the entropy change of an isothermal volume change from the slope of a constant-volume line; the G relation (∂s/∂p)T = −(∂v/∂T)p gives the entropy change of an isothermal pressure change from the slope of a constant-pressure line. With cp or cv for the temperature part, this is how entropy is tabulated for steam and refrigerants.

answer.pre:
(∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = −(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>,   v = RT/p   so   (∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = R/p
ds = −R dp/p   at constant T
Δs = −R ln(p₂/p₁) = −0.287 × ln 5 = −0.287 × 1.6094 = −0.4619 kJ/(kg·K)

answer: Real gas example. For a van der Waals gas (∂p/∂T)v = R/(v − b), so the A relation gives Δs = R·ln[(v₂ − b)/(v₁ − b)]: 5.946 J/(mol·K) for carbon dioxide doubling from 0.001 m³/mol at 300 K, against 5.763 J/(mol·K) for an ideal gas.

Closing check. The ideal-gas result agrees with the usual formula Δs = cpln(T₂/T₁) − R·ln(p₂/p₁) with T₂ = T₁: −0.4619 kJ/(kg·K). The negative sign is right, because compressing a gas at constant temperature lowers its entropy.

bank.q: Derive the Clapeyron equation from the equality of Gibbs functions of two phases in equilibrium. Reduce it to the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, stating the assumptions, and use the integrated form to estimate the saturation pressure of water at 323 K from 101.3 kPa at 373 K (h<sub>fg</sub> = 2257 kJ/kg, R = 0.4615 kJ/(kg·K)).
outline: g₁ = g₂ along the saturation line, so dg₁ = dg₂
dg = v dp − s dT for each phase
dp/dT = (s₁ − s₂)/(v₁ − v₂) = h₁₂/(T v₁₂)
Assume v<sub>f</sub> ≪ v<sub>g</sub> and ideal vapour: d ln p/dT = h<sub>fg</sub>/(RT²)
Integrate with constant h<sub>fg</sub>
Estimate 13.3 kPa against 12.35 kPa in the tables
answer: Equilibrium condition. Two phases of a pure substance at the same p and T are in equilibrium when their specific Gibbs functions are equal, g₁ = g₂. Along the saturation line this stays true, so for a small step along the line dg₁ = dg₂.

answer.text: Differentiate. For each phase dg = v dp − s dT:
answer.pre:
v₁dp − s₁dT = v₂dp − s₂dT
(v₁ − v₂)dp = (s₁ − s₂)dT
dp/dT = (s₁ − s₂)/(v₁ − v₂)

answer: Use the latent heat. The phase change happens at constant T and p, so the entropy change is the latent heat divided by T: s₁ − s₂ = h₁₂/T. This gives the Clapeyron equation dp/dT = h₁₂/(T·v₁₂). It is exact and holds for melting, boiling and sublimation.

answer.text: Clausius-Clapeyron form. For liquid and vapour well below the critical point, assume (i) vf ≪ vg, so vfg ≈ vg, and (ii) the vapour is an ideal gas, vg = RT/p:
answer.pre:
dp/dT = h<sub>fg</sub>/(T·RT/p) = p·h<sub>fg</sub>/(RT²)
d(ln p)/dT = h<sub>fg</sub>/(RT²)

answer: Integrate with hfg held constant (assumption iii): ln(p₂/p₁) = −(hfg/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).

Comparison. The steam tables give 12.35 kPa, so the estimate is about 8 % high. The main cause is assumption (iii): the real hfg grows to about 2382 kJ/kg at 323 K, which would make the exponent more negative and the pressure lower. Over a short range, say 353 to 373 K, the same method gives 48.2 kPa against 47.4 kPa in the tables, within 2 %.

bank.q: 25 kg of water at 95 °C is mixed adiabatically with 35 kg of water at 35 °C. The surroundings are at 15 °C. Taking c = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K), find the final temperature, the available energy of the water before and after mixing, the decrease in available energy, and the entropy generated.
outline: Energy balance gives the final temperature
Available energy of a body relative to T₀: AE = m c[(T − T₀) − T₀ ln(T/T₀)]
AE before = sum of the two, AE after for 60 kg at the mixed temperature
Decrease = T₀S<sub>gen</sub>
Check the two routes agree
answer: Data in kelvin. T₁ = 368.15 K (25 kg), T₂ = 308.15 K (35 kg), T₀ = 288.15 K, c = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K).

Final temperature. No heat or work leaves, so the heat lost by the hot water equals that gained by the cold: 25 × (368.15 − T) = 35 × (T − 308.15), so T = (25 × 368.15 + 35 × 308.15)/60 = 19 989/60 = 333.15 K (60 °C).
Available energy of a body. A body cooling from T to T₀ gives Q = m·c·(T − T₀) and gives up entropy m·c·ln(T/T₀), so AE = m·c·[(T − T₀) − T₀·ln(T/T₀)].
Decrease in available energy. 1079.5 − 799.1 = 280.4 kJ. No energy was lost (the mixing is adiabatic), but the hot water's heat has fallen in temperature.

Closing check. The two routes agree: the decrease in available energy, 280.4 kJ, equals T₀Sgen = 280.4 kJ, as the Gouy-Stodola theorem requires. About a quarter of the available energy (280.4/1079.5 = 26 %) is destroyed by mixing.

bank.q: Steam enters an adiabatic turbine at 3 MPa and 400 °C (h = 3231.7 kJ/kg, s = 6.9235 kJ/(kg·K)) and leaves at 100 kPa with dryness fraction 0.95. At 100 kPa, h<sub>f</sub> = 417.51, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2257.5 kJ/kg, s<sub>f</sub> = 1.3028, s<sub>fg</sub> = 6.0562 kJ/(kg·K). The dead state is water at 25 °C (h₀ = 104.83 kJ/kg, s₀ = 0.3672 kJ/(kg·K)) with T₀ = 298 K. Find the work, the flow exergy at inlet and outlet, the exergy destroyed, and the second law and isentropic efficiencies.
outline: Exit state from h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub> and s<sub>f</sub> + x s<sub>fg</sub>
w = h₁ − h₂
ψ = (h − h₀) − T₀(s − s₀) at inlet and outlet
i = T₀(s₂ − s₁); check w + i = ψ₁ − ψ₂
η<sub>II</sub> = w/(ψ₁ − ψ₂); η<sub>is</sub> from the isentropic exit state
Compare the two efficiencies
answer: Work. Adiabatic, steady, kinetic and potential energy neglected: w = h₁ − h₂ = 3231.7 − 2562.1 = 669.6 kJ/kg.
Exergy drop. ψ₁ − ψ₂ = 1173.1 − 464.0 = 709.1 kJ/kg: the most work any turbine could take from the steam between these two states.
Exergy destroyed. sgen = s₂ − s₁ = 7.0562 − 6.9235 = 0.1327 kJ/(kg·K), so i = T₀sgen = 298 × 0.1327 = 39.5 kJ/kg. Check: w + i = 669.6 + 39.5 = 709.1 kJ/kg = ψ₁ − ψ₂.
Second law efficiency. ηII = w/(ψ₁ − ψ₂) = 669.6/709.1 = 0.944.
Isentropic efficiency. The isentropic exit has s₂s = 6.9235: x₂s = (6.9235 − 1.3028)/6.0562 = 0.9281, h₂s = 417.51 + 0.9281 × 2257.5 = 2512.7 kJ/kg. ηis = (h₁ − h₂)/(h₁ − h₂s) = 669.6/719.0 = 0.931.

Comment. ηII (0.944) is higher than ηis (0.931). The isentropic loss h₂ − h₂s = 49.4 kJ/kg is larger than the exergy destroyed, 39.5 kJ/kg, because the extra enthalpy at the exit is at about 373 K, above T₀, and still carries some exergy (464.0 kJ/kg leaves with the steam, which a condenser or a lower stage could use).

bank.q: Derive the two TdS equations. Use them with a Maxwell relation to find the entropy and internal energy changes of a van der Waals gas in an isothermal expansion, and evaluate both for 1 mol of carbon dioxide (a = 0.364 Pa·m⁶/mol², b = 4.27 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol) expanding at 300 K from 0.001 to 0.002 m³/mol.
outline: s = s(T, v) and s = s(T, p)
c<sub>v</sub> = T(∂s/∂T)<sub>v</sub>, c<sub>p</sub> = T(∂s/∂T)<sub>p</sub>
Maxwell relations replace the entropy slopes
du = c<sub>v</sub>dT + [T(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> − p]dv
van der Waals: Δs = R ln[(v₂ − b)/(v₁ − b)], Δu = a(1/v₁ − 1/v₂)
Numbers: 5.946 J/(mol·K), 182 J/mol

answer.text: First TdS equation. Take s = s(T, v):
answer.pre:
ds = (∂s/∂T)<sub>v</sub>dT + (∂s/∂v)<sub>T</sub>dv
(∂s/∂T)<sub>v</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>/T          (from c<sub>v</sub> = (∂u/∂T)<sub>v</sub> and du = T ds at constant v)
(∂s/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub>      (Maxwell, from A)
T ds = c<sub>v</sub>dT + T(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub>dv

answer.text: Second TdS equation. Take s = s(T, p):
answer.pre:
ds = (∂s/∂T)<sub>p</sub>dT + (∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub>dp
(∂s/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>/T          (from c<sub>p</sub> = (∂h/∂T)<sub>p</sub> and dh = T ds at constant p)
(∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = −(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>     (Maxwell, from G)
T ds = c<sub>p</sub>dT − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>dp

answer: Energy relation. Put the first TdS equation into du = T ds − p dv: du = cvdT + [T(∂p/∂T)v − p]dv. At constant T only the bracket remains.
van der Waals gas. p = RT/(v − b) − a/v², so (∂p/∂T)v = R/(v − b). At constant T: ds = R dv/(v − b), and T(∂p/∂T)v − p = RT/(v − b) − RT/(v − b) + a/v² = a/v², so du = a dv/v².
Integrate. Δs = R·ln[(v₂ − b)/(v₁ − b)] and Δu = a(1/v₁ − 1/v₂).

Interpretation. The real gas gains about 3.2 % more entropy than an ideal gas, because only v − b of its volume is free space. Its internal energy rises by 182 J/mol at constant temperature, the work done against molecular attraction; an ideal gas would have Δu = 0.
Closing check. As a → 0 and b → 0 the results reduce to Δs = R·ln(v₂/v₁) and Δu = 0, the ideal-gas values, as they must.

bank.q: The saturation pressure of water is 47.4 kPa at 80 °C and 101.3 kPa at 100 °C. Using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, estimate the latent heat of vaporisation in this range (R = 0.4615 kJ/(kg·K)) and compare it with the steam-table value of 2282.5 kJ/kg at 90 °C. Also show what a cruder estimate from the straight-line slope Δp/ΔT gives, and explain the difference.
outline: Integrated form solved for h<sub>fg</sub>
Kelvin temperatures
h<sub>fg</sub> ≈ 2309 kJ/kg, about 1 % above the table
Secant slope with v<sub>g</sub> = RT/p at the mean point gives about 2206 kJ/kg
The curve is not straight, so the integrated form is better
answer: Data in kelvin. T₁ = 353.15 K, p₁ = 47.4 kPa; T₂ = 373.15 K, p₂ = 101.3 kPa.
Solve the integrated form for hfg. ln(p₂/p₁) = −(hfg/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁) = (hfg/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂), so hfg = R·ln(p₂/p₁)/(1/T₁ − 1/T₂).

Compare. 2309 against 2282.5 kJ/kg at 90 °C: about 1.2 % high. The result is an average over 80 to 100 °C (the table gives about 2308 at 80 °C and 2257 at 100 °C), and the ideal-vapour assumption adds a small error.

answer.text: Cruder estimate with the Clapeyron equation and a straight-line slope at the midpoint (90 °C, mean pressure 74.35 kPa):

answer: Why the cruder one is worse. The vapour-pressure curve bends upward, so the arithmetic mean pressure (74.35 kPa) is above the true saturation pressure at 90 °C (70.2 kPa in the tables). That makes vg too small, and the estimate comes out about 3 % low. The integrated form follows the curvature of ln p, so it is the better method.
Closing check. Put hfg = 2309 kJ/kg back into the integrated form from 373.15 K: p at 353.15 K = 101.3 × e−(2309/0.4615) × 1.5177 × 10⁻⁴ = 101.3 × e−0.7594 = 47.4 kPa, the given value.

bank.q: Define the volume expansivity and the isothermal and isentropic compressibilities. Derive the Mayer relation c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = Tvβ²/κ<sub>T</sub> and the ratio c<sub>p</sub>/c<sub>v</sub> = κ<sub>T</sub>/κ<sub>s</sub>. Show that c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R for an ideal gas, and find c<sub>v</sub> of water at 25 °C (v = 0.001003 m³/kg, β = 2.57 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, κ<sub>T</sub> = 4.52 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹, c<sub>p</sub> = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K)).
outline: β = (1/v)(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>; κ<sub>T</sub> = −(1/v)(∂v/∂p)<sub>T</sub>; κ<sub>s</sub> = −(1/v)(∂v/∂p)<sub>s</sub>
Subtract the TdS equations and use the cyclic relation
c<sub>p</sub> ≥ c<sub>v</sub>; equal where β = 0
Ideal gas reduces to R
TdS equations at constant s give κ<sub>T</sub>/κ<sub>s</sub>
Water: 0.0437 kJ/(kg·K), c<sub>v</sub> = 4.136
answer: Definitions. β = (1/v)(∂v/∂T)p in 1/K; κT = −(1/v)(∂v/∂p)T in 1/Pa; κs = −(1/v)(∂v/∂p)s in 1/Pa. The minus signs make the compressibilities positive.

answer.text: Mayer relation. Subtract the two TdS equations and hold v fixed:
answer.pre:
T ds = c<sub>v</sub>dT + T(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub>dv = c<sub>p</sub>dT − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>dp
(c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub>)dT = T(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub>dv + T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>dp
at constant v:  c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub>

c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = −T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>²/(∂v/∂p)<sub>T</sub>
(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = vβ,   (∂v/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = −vκ<sub>T</sub>
c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = T(vβ)²/(vκ<sub>T</sub>) = Tvβ²/κ<sub>T</sub>

answer: Consequences. T, v and κT are positive and β² ≥ 0, so cp ≥ cv for every substance, with equality where β = 0 (water near 4 °C).
Ideal gas. v = RT/p gives β = 1/T and κT = 1/p, so Tvβ²/κT = T × (RT/p) × (1/T²) × p = R. For air, cp − cv = 1.005 − 0.718 = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K) = R.

Ratio of specific heats. At constant s both TdS equations equal zero: cvdT = −T(∂p/∂T)vdv and cpdT = T(∂v/∂T)pdp. Dividing, cp/cv = −[(∂v/∂T)p/(∂p/∂T)v](∂p/∂v)s. By the cyclic relation the bracket is −(∂v/∂p)T, so cp/cv = (∂v/∂p)T/(∂v/∂p)s = κT/κs.
Closing check. For a liquid cp and cv differ by about 1 %, so tables quote a single "c" for water; for air they differ by R, about 40 % of cv (0.287/0.718 = 0.40).

bank.q: Define the Joule-Thomson coefficient and derive μ<sub>JT</sub> = [T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> − v]/c<sub>p</sub>. Show that it is zero for an ideal gas, explain the inversion temperature, and estimate the temperature change of nitrogen throttled from 20 bar to 1 bar at 300 K using μ<sub>JT</sub> ≈ (2a/RT − b)/c<sub>p,m</sub> (a = 0.137 Pa·m⁶/mol², b = 3.87 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol, c<sub>p,m</sub> = 29.1 J/(mol·K)).
outline: Throttling: adiabatic, no work, so h₁ = h₂
μ<sub>JT</sub> = (∂T/∂p)<sub>h</sub>
dh = c<sub>p</sub>dT + [v − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>]dp with dh = 0
Ideal gas T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = v, so μ<sub>JT</sub> = 0
Inversion curve and T<sub>i</sub> = 2a/(Rb) for a van der Waals gas
Nitrogen: 0.245 K/bar, about −4.6 K, T<sub>i</sub> ≈ 852 K
answer: Throttling. Flow through a valve or porous plug is adiabatic, does no work and changes the kinetic energy very little, so the steady-flow energy equation gives h₁ = h₂. The Joule-Thomson coefficient is μJT = (∂T/∂p)h, the temperature change per unit pressure change at constant enthalpy.

answer.text: Derivation. Write h = h(T, p) and use the enthalpy relation from the second TdS equation:
answer.pre:
dh = c<sub>p</sub>dT + [v − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>]dp
at constant h:  0 = c<sub>p</sub>dT + [v − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>]dp
μ<sub>JT</sub> = (∂T/∂p)<sub>h</sub> = [T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> − v]/c<sub>p</sub> = v(Tβ − 1)/c<sub>p</sub>

answer: Ideal gas. v = RT/p gives T(∂v/∂T)p = T·R/p = v, so μJT = 0. Throttling an ideal gas lowers its pressure but not its temperature, because its enthalpy depends on temperature only.

Real gas and inversion. Pressure always falls in a throttle, so μJT > 0 means cooling and μJT < 0 means warming. The states where μJT = 0 form the inversion curve on a T–p diagram, and its highest temperature is the maximum inversion temperature. A gas must be below it for throttling to cool it.
van der Waals estimate. At low pressure μJT ≈ (2a/RT − b)/cp,m: attraction (a) makes the gas cool, molecular size (b) makes it warm. Setting it to zero gives Ti = 2a/(Rb).

Closing check. Units: (m³/mol)/(J/(mol·K)) = m³·K/J = K/Pa, as a temperature change per pressure change should be. 300 K is far below 852 K, so the positive sign (cooling) is consistent. The van der Waals inversion temperature is an overestimate; the measured maximum for nitrogen is lower, near 620 K, but still far above room temperature.

bank.q: A room must be kept at 22 °C (295 K) when the outside air is at 5 °C (278 K); it needs 10 kW of heat. Compare an electric heater, a heat pump with a COP of 3.5, and a reversible heat pump by their work input, exergy destroyed and second law efficiency. Explain why the heater's first-law efficiency of 100 % hides its waste.
outline: Exergy of the heat delivered: Q(1 − T₀/T<sub>room</sub>)
Heater: W = Q, η<sub>II</sub> about 5.8 %
Heat pump COP 3.5: W = 2.857 kW, η<sub>II</sub> about 20 %
Reversible: COP = T/(T − T₀) = 17.35, η<sub>II</sub> = 1
Exergy destroyed = W − exergy delivered
First-law efficiency counts kJ, not their quality
answer: Reference. Take the outside air as the surroundings, T₀ = 278 K. The 10 kW of heat is delivered at T = 295 K.
Exergy of the heat delivered. ẊQ = Q̇(1 − T₀/T) = 10 × (1 − 278/295) = 10 × 0.05763 = 0.576 kW. This is the least work any device could use to keep the room warm.
Electric heater. All 10 kW of heat comes from 10 kW of electricity, which is pure exergy. Exergy destroyed = 10 − 0.576 = 9.42 kW; ηII = 0.576/10 = 5.8 %.

Heat pump, COP 3.5. Work W = Q/COP = 10/3.5 = 2.857 kW. The heat pump also takes 10 − 2.857 = 7.143 kW from the outside air, which carries no exergy because it is at T₀. Exergy destroyed = 2.857 − 0.576 = 2.28 kW; ηII = 0.576/2.857 = 20.2 %.
Reversible heat pump. COPrev = T/(T − T₀) = 295/17 = 17.35, so W = 10/17.35 = 0.576 kW, equal to the exergy delivered. Exergy destroyed = 0; ηII = 1.

Why the first law misleads. The heater's energy balance is perfect: 10 kW in, 10 kW out. But it turns high-quality energy (electricity) into low-quality energy (heat only 17 K above the surroundings), destroying 9.42 kW of exergy. The second law efficiency exposes this; it also shows that even a good heat pump (ηII = 0.20) has room to improve.
Closing check. ηII of the heat pump also equals COP/COPrev = 3.5/17.35 = 0.202, the same as the exergy route.

bank.q: Use the Clapeyron equation to find the slope of the ice-water melting line at 273.15 K (h<sub>sf</sub> = 333.5 kJ/kg, v<sub>ice</sub> = 0.0010908, v<sub>water</sub> = 0.0010002 m³/kg) and of the water-steam line at 100 °C (h<sub>fg</sub> = 2257 kJ/kg, v<sub>g</sub> = 1.672, v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001043 m³/kg). Explain the signs, estimate the melting point at 10 MPa, and check the boiling-line slope against saturation pressures of 84.61 kPa at 95 °C and 120.90 kPa at 105 °C.
outline: Clapeyron: dp/dT = h₁₂/(T v₁₂) from equal Gibbs functions
Melting: v<sub>sf</sub> < 0 so dp/dT ≈ −1.35 × 10⁷ Pa/K
Melting point at 10 MPa about −0.73 °C
Boiling: dp/dT ≈ 3.62 kPa/K
Table secant 3.63 kPa/K agrees
Sign follows the sign of the volume change
answer: The equation. Equal Gibbs functions along a phase boundary give dp/dT = h₁₂/(T·v₁₂) (the Clapeyron equation), with h₁₂ the latent heat and v₁₂ the volume change in the same direction (for example liquid minus solid with the heat of melting).

Melting point at 10 MPa. Δp = 10 × 10⁶ − 101 325 = 9.90 × 10⁶ Pa, so ΔT = −7.42 × 10⁻⁸ × 9.90 × 10⁶ = −0.73 K: ice melts at about 272.4 K (−0.73 °C). The line is so steep that pressure has only a small effect.

Check with the tables. The secant slope from 95 °C to 105 °C is (120.90 − 84.61)/10 = 3.63 kPa/K, within 0.3 % of the Clapeyron value. The exact equation needs no ideal-gas assumption, so it agrees closely when table values of v are used.

Why the signs differ. The latent heat is positive in both cases (heat is taken in on melting and on boiling), so the sign of dp/dT is the sign of the volume change. Steam takes far more room than water, so the boiling line slopes forward. Ice takes more room than water, so vsf is negative and the melting line slopes backward: raising the pressure favours the denser phase, liquid water, and lowers the melting point. Most other substances shrink on freezing, and their melting lines slope forward.

Judgement. The two slopes differ by a factor of about 3700 (1.35 × 10⁷ against 3.62 × 10³ Pa/K). Pressure moves the boiling point strongly (a pressure cooker at 2 bar boils near 120 °C) but the melting point hardly at all, so claims that skating works only by pressure melting should be treated with care: 10 MPa lowers the melting point by under one kelvin.
Closing check. 1 atm × dT/dp = 101 325 × (−7.42 × 10⁻⁸) = −0.0075 K, the figure usually quoted for ice.

glossary.def: The very large body around the system, at T₀ and p₀, that can take or give heat without changing temperature.
Another name for unavailable energy: the part of energy that can never become work in given surroundings.
Another name for exergy, used in many syllabi.
Another name for exergy destroyed, I = T₀S<sub>gen</sub>.
Work done by a closed system minus the work spent pushing back the atmosphere, W − p₀(V₂ − V₁).
The largest useful work between two given states, obtained on a fully reversible path.
Entropy created inside a real process; never negative and zero only for a reversible process.
Actual work of a turbine divided by the work of an isentropic turbine between the same inlet state and exit pressure.
The state of a simple compressible substance is fixed by two independent properties.
A quantity that depends only on the state, such as p, T, u or s; its differential is exact.
A quantity that depends on the path between states, such as heat and work.
A factor that turns an inexact differential into an exact one; 1/T turns δq<sub>rev</sub> into ds.
The two properties that each potential depends on most simply: S, V for U; S, p for H; T, V for A; T, p for G.
The Gibbs function per mole of a substance; equal in two phases in equilibrium.
Any of U, H, A and G, whose fall at fixed natural variables bounds the work of a process.
The curve on a p–T diagram along which two phases coexist in equilibrium.
Melting of ice under pressure and refreezing when the pressure is removed.
κ<sub>s</sub> = −(1/v)(∂v/∂p)<sub>s</sub>; fixes the speed of sound.
The inverse of a compressibility: the pressure rise per fractional decrease of volume.
Flow through a valve or porous plug with no heat, no work and no change of kinetic energy, so h₁ = h₂.
The states where μ<sub>JT</sub> = 0; its highest temperature is the maximum inversion temperature.
p = RT/(v − b) − a/v²: a gas model with molecular attraction a and molecular volume b.
